listings.realcost: Roughly $10/week, $25/month, or ~$60/year on the usual promo — before you can apply to anything.
free_includes: Nothing without paying — browsing previews only
paid_locked: The skills tests and resume reviews
listings.short: No. FlexJobs charges job seekers a subscription before they can see or apply to its hand-screened remote listings. People keep searching 'FlexJobs free' — there is no free tier, only previews.
listings.catch: You're paying for curation — a scam-filtered remote job board. That's a real service, but it inverts the normal deal: the seeker funds the board. Auto-renewal is on by default.
listings.worth: The screened listings largely exist free elsewhere (company sites, Remote OK, LinkedIn) — you're buying the filtering and the time it saves.
smart_moves: If you buy it, buy one month during an active search — not the annual plan — and turn off auto-renew immediately
Check Remote OK and We Work Remotely first; the overlap is large
listings.get_summary: In practice: a paid, scam-screened remote job board that a lot of people arrive at expecting to be free. It isn't.
drawbacks: No free tier at all
Auto-renewing subscription
Much of the inventory is findable free elsewhere
more_info: Is FlexJobs a scam?
No — it's a legitimate paid service with real, screened listings. The trap is expectation: it markets to people searching for free remote-job help, then charges at the door.

listings.name: Remote OK
listings.limits: None for seekers — browse and apply straight to the employer
listings.realcost: Nothing. Employers pay to post.
free_includes: Browse every remote job listing — no account, no card
Apply directly on the employer's own page
Salary ranges shown on many listings
paid_locked: Nothing for seekers — employers pay for postings and highlights
listings.short: Yes — fully open: every remote listing is browsable and applications go straight to the employer, no account, no card, no wall. Employers pay to post; seekers pay nothing.
listings.catch: It's a firehose, not a concierge — tech-heavy inventory, minimal screening compared to paid boards, and the site is dense with promoted listings.
listings.worth: Paid boards charge seekers ~$60/year for a comparable remote-jobs feed; this one is $0.
smart_moves: Filter by salary-disclosed listings first — they correlate with serious employers
listings.get_summary: In practice: a genuinely open remote-jobs board — the thing people hope FlexJobs is.
drawbacks: Tech-skewed inventory
Light screening — do your own diligence
Ad-dense layout
more_info: Remote OK vs FlexJobs?
Same category, opposite models: Remote OK is free for seekers and funded by employers; FlexJobs charges seekers for curation. Start free; pay only if the filtering earns it.

listings.name: Feedly
listings.autobill: Only if you subscribe to Pro
listings.limits: Up to 100 sources in 3 folders; search and AI features are paid
listings.realcost: Nothing at the free tier. Pro starts around $6-8/month.
free_includes: Follow up to 100 sources in 3 folders
Web and mobile apps that sync
The basic magazine-style reading experience
paid_locked: Integrations (Evernote, IFTTT, Zapier) and hiding sponsored cards
listings.short: Yes — a real permanent free tier: 100 sources, 3 folders, solid apps. But search inside your own feeds is paywalled, which stings once your archive matters, and the upgrade prompts are constant.
listings.catch: 100 sources sounds like plenty until it isn't, and not being able to search your own feeds is the squeeze that converts people. Sponsored cards appear in the free reading flow.
listings.worth: Pro is ~$72-96/year; casual readers genuinely don't need it.
smart_moves: Prune dead feeds to stay under the 100-source cap
Pair the free tier with your browser's find-on-page instead of paying just for search
listings.get_summary: In practice: the mainstream RSS reader's real free tier — comfortable for casual following, deliberately cramped for power users.
drawbacks: No search on free
100-source cap
Sponsored cards and persistent upsells
more_info: Is RSS still worth using?
More than ever — it's the algorithm-free way to follow sources directly. Every reader listed here consumes the same open feeds, so you can switch readers without losing anything.

listings.name: Inoreader
listings.limits: Up to 150 feeds with ads; rules, monitoring and full search are paid
listings.realcost: Nothing at the free tier — you read with ads. Paid plans from roughly $7.50/month.
free_includes: Follow up to 150 feeds, with ads
Web and mobile apps with sync
Basic folders and tagging
paid_locked: Full-archive search, and removing the ads
listings.short: Yes — one of the roomier free tiers in RSS: 150 feeds, real apps, folders. The price is ads in your reading flow, and the genuinely powerful stuff (rules, monitoring, search) is paid.
listings.catch: Ads inside a reading app annoy exactly the kind of person who uses RSS; that's the nudge. Power features are firmly paywalled.
listings.worth: Comparable paid plans run ~$90/year; the free tier covers ordinary daily reading.
smart_moves: Use folders aggressively — the free tier's organization is better than most rivals'
listings.get_summary: In practice: a generous, ad-supported free reader whose paid tiers chase the power users.
drawbacks: Ads in the free reading flow
Automation and search are paid
150-feed cap
more_info: Feedly or Inoreader free?
Inoreader's free tier is roomier (150 feeds vs 100) and has ads; Feedly's is cleaner-looking but caps harder. Both read the same open RSS — try both, keep one.

listings.name: NewsBlur
listings.limits: Up to 64 sites free; the premium that lifts it is one of the cheapest in software
listings.realcost: Nothing for 64 sites. Premium is about $36/year.
free_includes: Read up to 64 sites with training and filtering
The 'training' system that hides what you don't care about
Web, iOS and Android apps — open source
listings.short: Yes — 64 sites free, forever, from a one-developer operation that's been quietly reliable for over a decade. The cap is honest and the paid tier that lifts it costs less than most apps' monthly fee, per year.
listings.catch: 64 sites is a genuine ceiling for heavy readers, and the interface has an old-forum charm that isn't for everyone.
listings.worth: Premium is ~$36/year — the 'squeeze' here is about as gentle as paid software gets.
smart_moves: Train it early — the hide-this filtering is the actual killer feature
If you pass 64 feeds, the annual fee is cheaper than the time you'll spend working around it
listings.get_summary: In practice: an honest indie RSS reader — real free tier, cheap upgrade, no dark patterns.
drawbacks: 64-site cap
Dated interface
Small team means slower feature pace
more_info: Who runs NewsBlur?
Essentially one developer, openly, since 2009 — the code is open source. That's the opposite failure profile of VC-funded readers that pivot or fold.

listings.name: The Old Reader
listings.limits: Up to 100 feeds; search and no-ads need the ~$3/month premium
listings.realcost: Nothing for 100 feeds and the classic reading experience.
free_includes: Follow up to 100 feeds in a clean, Google-Reader-style UI
Sharing and comments with friends who also use it
Import your subscriptions from any reader (OPML)
paid_locked: Faster feed refresh and no ads
listings.short: Yes — it exists specifically to be what Google Reader was: simple, fast, 100 feeds free. Premium is a modest ~$3/month for search and a higher cap.
listings.catch: Deliberately basic — no AI, no automation, minimal apps (it's web-first). If you want power features, this isn't where they live.
listings.worth: It replaces a product people still mourn, for $0.
smart_moves: Export/import via OPML — your subscriptions are portable between every reader on this list
listings.get_summary: In practice: the Google Reader experience, alive and free at 100 feeds.
drawbacks: Web-first, thin mobile story
No power features by design
100-feed cap
more_info: Why do people still want Google Reader?
Because a chronological list of exactly what you chose to follow — no ranking, no engagement bait — turned out to be the healthiest way to read the web. RSS never died; the readers just got quieter.

listings.name: Microsoft Copilot
listings.autobill: Only if you subscribe to Pro
listings.account: Microsoft account for full features; basic use without
listings.limits: Usage caps at busy times; newest models and Office integration sit in Pro
listings.realcost: Nothing for everyday chat and image help. Pro is $20/month.
free_includes: The mainstream assistant free in Windows, Edge, Bing and the app
Chat, image generation, and web-grounded answers
No card at any point on the free tier
paid_locked: Priority access at peak times and the newest models
Copilot in Word, Excel and Outlook (Pro / Microsoft 365)
listings.short: Yes — Microsoft's assistant is genuinely free for everyday use across Windows, Edge and the app, with image generation included. Pro buys peak-time priority and Office integration.
listings.catch: It's woven into Windows whether you asked for it or not, it leans on a Microsoft account, and the free tier gets deprioritized when demand spikes. Your prompts feed the product.
listings.worth: Pro is $240/year; the free tier covers most people's actual usage.
smart_moves: Use it signed-in for history, signed-out for quick anonymous checks
If you only want Office AI occasionally, a single month of Pro beats a subscription
listings.get_summary: In practice: a capable free assistant already sitting in the software most people use all day.
drawbacks: Deprioritized at peak times
Pushes Microsoft account and Pro
Embedded in Windows by default
more_info: Copilot free vs ChatGPT free?
Similar engines under the hood. Copilot's free tier is more generous with web-grounded answers and images; ChatGPT's app ecosystem is bigger. Both are real free tiers.

listings.name: DeepSeek
listings.limits: Generous daily use; the open-weights models are free to download outright
listings.realcost: Nothing for chat. The models themselves are MIT-licensed — free even commercially.
free_includes: Free chat with a frontier-class model, web and app
The model weights themselves, MIT-licensed, free to run yourself
Reasoning mode included on the free tier
paid_locked: Only the developer API bills — by usage, cheaply
listings.short: Yes — unusually so. The chat is free with generous limits, and unlike every Western lab, the underlying models are open-weights under MIT: you can download and run them yourself, even commercially.
listings.catch: The hosted service runs on servers in China and your conversations are subject to Chinese data law and content filtering. Privacy-sensitive users should run the open weights locally instead — that's the genuinely free path.
listings.worth: Comparable Western frontier access runs $20/month; here both the service and the weights are $0.
smart_moves: Treat the hosted chat as public — or run the weights locally via Ollama/LM Studio for real privacy
The distilled small models run on ordinary laptops
listings.get_summary: In practice: frontier-class AI where 'free' includes the model itself, with a data-jurisdiction trade-off on the hosted version.
drawbacks: Hosted data goes through China
Content filtering on political topics
API (not chat) is the paid surface
more_info: What does open-weights actually get me?
The model file itself. You can run it on your own hardware, offline, forever, commercially — no account, no terms changes, no shutdown risk. That's freer than any hosted free tier.

safety.verdict: Capable and free — and the data question here is different from the others, so answer it deliberately.
safety.download: The official apps and deepseek.com. Wrapper apps charging for it are common.
safety.data: The company is Chinese and its consumer service stores user data on servers in China under Chinese law. Several governments have restricted the app on official devices for that reason. This is a jurisdiction question, not an accusation — but it should decide what you type into it.
safety.scams: The open-weight models are genuinely open and can be run locally, which is the way to use it if the jurisdiction concerns you.
safety.account_risk: Treat anything you send as leaving your control. That's true of every hosted AI service; the variable here is which legal system it lands in.

listings.name: NotebookLM
listings.limits: Caps on notebooks and sources per notebook; higher caps in the paid Plus tier
listings.realcost: Nothing at the free tier.
free_includes: Upload your documents and query them with citations
Audio Overviews — the two-host podcast summaries
Real source-grounded answers, not open-web guessing
paid_locked: Higher notebook/source caps and team features (Plus)
listings.short: Yes — Google's research notebook is free with a Google account: upload sources, ask questions, get cited answers, generate the podcast-style audio summaries. Plus mainly raises caps.
listings.catch: Everything routes through your Google account, caps are real for heavy research use, and Google has a history of retiring experiments — don't make it your only archive.
listings.worth: The closest paid equivalents are $20/month research tools; the free tier does the core job.
smart_moves: Keep master copies of your sources elsewhere — treat it as a lens, not a library
Audio Overviews are the standout: feed it a dense PDF before a commute
listings.get_summary: In practice: a genuinely free grounded-research tool — your documents, cited answers, audio summaries.
drawbacks: Google account required
Source and notebook caps
Experiment-status product risk
more_info: How is this different from ChatGPT?
It only answers from the sources you give it, with citations — which means far fewer invented facts, and it's actually checkable.

listings.name: Stable Diffusion
listings.limits: Your own hardware: a mid-range GPU (or patience) is the real requirement
listings.realcost: Nothing for the models. Hosted convenience services charge — the local route doesn't.
free_includes: Open-weights image generation you run on your own machine
Unlimited generations — no credits, no watermark, no queue
A huge free ecosystem: ComfyUI, Automatic1111, community models
paid_locked: Nothing locally — hosted front-ends (DreamStudio etc.) sell convenience
listings.short: Yes — the genuinely free image generator: open weights you download and run locally, unlimited, no account, no credits. The cost is hardware and setup, not money.
listings.catch: The free path assumes a decent GPU and an evening of setup. Every polished website offering 'free Stable Diffusion' is a credit-metered business — the freedom is in the local install, not the hosted wrappers.

smart_moves: Start with ComfyUI or A1111 and a community model from a model hub
No GPU? A used 8–12GB card pays for itself in three months of subscription prices
listings.get_summary: In practice: unlimited image generation for the price of your own electricity — the open-weights answer to Midjourney.
drawbacks: Needs a real GPU and technical setup
Quality depends on the model/workflow you pick
Hosted wrappers reintroduce credits and fees
more_info: Stable Diffusion vs Midjourney?
Midjourney is easier and has no free tier at all; SD is free forever but you do the setup. If you generate regularly, local SD is the only path where volume costs nothing.

listings.name: Character.AI
listings.autobill: Only if you subscribe to c.ai+
listings.limits: Free chat is effectively unlimited; queues and ads appear at peak, faster responses are paid
listings.realcost: Nothing in money. Attention and hours are the actual price.
free_includes: Unlimited character chat on the free tier
Creating your own characters
Community characters and group chats
listings.short: Yes — the free tier is real and effectively unlimited; c.ai+ sells speed and priority rather than unlocking the product. The business runs on your engagement, not your card.
listings.catch: It's engineered to keep you talking — the 'free' here is paid in hours. Filters are strict and shift without notice, and conversations train the system. Not a privacy surface for anything personal.
listings.worth: c.ai+ is ~$120/year for impatience; the product itself is free.
smart_moves: Treat every conversation as logged and analyzed — because it is
If response queues annoy you, off-peak hours beat paying
listings.get_summary: In practice: genuinely free entertainment chat whose real cost is measured in time, not dollars.
drawbacks: Engagement-optimized by design
Strict, changeable content filters
Conversations feed training
more_info: Why is it so free?
Scale and engagement are the product — your hours and conversations are worth more to the company than a subscription wall would be.

sentiment.split: Google Play 2.0/5 across roughly 2.4 million ratings — the lowest score of any listing on this site.
sentiment.praised: The technology impresses users, and the free tier is genuinely unlimited in a way paid rivals aren't — reviewers describe conversations that feel sustained and characterful.
sentiment.complained: The score is driven by organised anger at content filtering that tightened repeatedly, changed without notice, and altered characters people had spent months building. Separately and more seriously, the company has faced lawsuits over harms to minors and has since restricted teen access — a safety record that belongs in any assessment of it.
sentiment.takeaway: A 2.0 from 2.4 million people is not a normal review distribution; it's a user base in revolt over changes to a free product. Free here is paid in hours, and the conversations are training data — treat it as entertainment, never as a confidant.

safety.verdict: This is the one listing on this site where we'd give a qualified no, and it isn't about money.
safety.data: Conversations are stored and used to improve the system. Nothing you tell a character should be treated as private, and that includes anything about your health, your relationships, or your location.
safety.account_risk: The product is engineered for engagement, and the review record is full of people describing hours they didn't intend to spend. The company has faced lawsuits over harms to minors and has since restricted access for teenagers.
safety.scams: No financial scam — the free tier is real. The cost is time, attention, and the data in the conversations.
safety.download: The official apps and character.ai. Unofficial clients asking for your login are credential theft.

listings.name: Suno

listings.realcost: Nothing in money — but free-tier songs aren't yours to monetize.
free_includes: Full song generation — vocals, lyrics, arrangement — on daily credits
Enough daily allowance to genuinely play and prototype
paid_locked: Commercial use of what you make

listings.catch: The rights, not the credits, are the real wall: free-tier output is non-commercial. If a song matters to you, you need the subscription that covers it — that's the squeeze working as designed.
listings.worth: Paid plans run ~$10–30/month; for casual play the daily free credits are honestly generous.
smart_moves: Prototype free, subscribe only for the month you produce something you'll publish
Read the rights terms before putting a free-tier song anywhere monetized
listings.get_summary: In practice: real free song-making for fun — with ownership of the results as the paid product.
drawbacks: No commercial rights on free output
Daily credit ceiling
Ongoing industry litigation around training data
more_info: Can I put free-tier Suno songs on YouTube?
On a non-monetized channel, generally yes under their terms; monetized use needs a paid plan. Terms shift — check before publishing.

listings.name: ElevenLabs

listings.realcost: Nothing in money for light use — attribution and tight quota are the price.
free_includes: Best-in-class text-to-speech on a monthly quota
A taste of voice design and the voice library

For long-form free TTS, pair it with a local engine and save ElevenLabs for the parts that matter
