Attribution required on free output
Cloning and volume are paid
more_info: Is there a truly free ElevenLabs alternative?
Local open models (Piper, XTTS-class) are free and unlimited but a clear step down in naturalness. The gap is why the meter works.

listings.name: Grok
listings.autobill: Only via X Premium / SuperGrok subscriptions
listings.limits: A capped number of free messages per window; higher limits ride on X Premium or SuperGrok
listings.realcost: Nothing in money for light use — an X account and your data are the entry fee.
free_includes: A capped free allowance of chat and image generation
Real-time X/Twitter data in answers — its distinctive trick
paid_locked: Newest model versions and heavy features
listings.short: Sort of — there's a real free allowance, but it's tightly capped and exists inside the X ecosystem: account required, usage data feeding the platform, and the paid tiers doing the heavy lifting.
listings.catch: The free tier is a funnel into X Premium/SuperGrok subscriptions, caps shift without much notice, and your prompts default into the training pipeline unless you opt out in settings.
listings.worth: Comparable capped-free chat exists at every rival without requiring a social-network account; the X-data angle is the only unique free value.
smart_moves: Opt out of data training in settings first thing
Use the free cap for the X-realtime questions rivals can't answer; do everything else on a roomier free tier
listings.get_summary: In practice: a capped free taste of X's chatbot, priced in account linkage and data rather than dollars.
drawbacks: Tight, shifting free caps
Tied to the X ecosystem
Training opt-out is buried in settings
more_info: Grok free vs ChatGPT free?
ChatGPT's free tier is roomier and standalone. Grok's one edge is live X data — if you don't need that, the account requirement buys you nothing.

listings.name: Wikidata & Wikimedia dumps
listings.limits: None on the dumps; API has courtesy rate limits
listings.realcost: Nothing. A nonprofit publishes its entire database on purpose.
free_includes: The full Wikidata graph as downloadable JSON and RDF
Complete Wikipedia article dumps in every language
A live query service (SPARQL) with no key
CC0 licensing on Wikidata — no attribution required
listings.short: Yes, completely. Wikimedia publishes its whole database as free downloads — no key, no account, no rate card. Wikidata is CC0, so you can use it commercially without even crediting it.
listings.catch: There is no catch on price. The catch is size: the full dumps run to tens of gigabytes compressed, so you need a plan for storage and parsing before you start.
listings.worth: A commercial knowledge graph of this scope is a five-figure annual licence. This is a free download.
smart_moves: Take the truthy subset rather than the full dump unless you need history — it's a fraction of the size
Use the SPARQL endpoint for exploring, dumps for production — the endpoint has timeouts by design
Mirror from a regional mirror rather than hammering the primary server
listings.get_summary: In practice: the single best free structured-data source on the internet, and the one most projects should start from.
drawbacks: Full dumps are large enough to need real disk and real patience
Data quality varies by topic — it's crowd-maintained
The query service enforces timeouts on expensive queries
more_info: Why CC0 matters more than it sounds

Most 'open' data carries a share-alike or attribution licence that quietly infects whatever you build with it. Wikidata is CC0 — public domain dedication — so it can go into a commercial product with no licence obligations at all. That is rarer than it should be, and it is the reason Wikidata ends up underneath so many other services.
Dumps versus the API

The API and query service are for exploring and for light live lookups; they are rate-limited as a courtesy to everyone else. If your job is bulk — building an index, training something, joining against your own data — take the dump. Downloading once is kinder and faster than a million polite requests.

listings.name: OpenStreetMap
listings.limits: None on the data; tile servers have a usage policy
listings.realcost: Nothing. Attribution under the ODbL licence is the only obligation.
free_includes: The entire world map as downloadable data (planet file and regional extracts)
Geocoding through Nominatim with no key
Routing, tiles and editing tools built on top
Commercial use permitted under ODbL
paid_locked: Nothing — though hosted providers sell convenience on top
listings.short: Yes. The map data is free to download and free to use commercially, with attribution. It's the reason a mapping product doesn't have to mean a Google bill.
listings.catch: The data is free; serving it at scale is not. The community tile and geocoding servers run on donations and have a usage policy — build anything real and you self-host or pay a hosting provider.
listings.worth: The direct replacement for Google Maps Platform, whose bills start at zero and don't stay there.
smart_moves: Take a regional extract from Geofabrik rather than the whole planet file
Never point a production app at the community Nominatim or tile servers — that's the one rule everyone breaks
ODbL is share-alike for derived databases; read it before you mix it into a proprietary dataset
listings.get_summary: In practice: the world's map, yours to download, with a licence that permits business use.
drawbacks: Coverage quality varies sharply by region
Self-hosting tiles or geocoding is real infrastructure work
ODbL's share-alike terms need reading if you're building a product
more_info: The usage policy is the actual catch

The free community servers exist so people can learn and prototype. Pointing an app with real users at them will get you blocked, and rightly — you'd be spending a donation-funded budget. Either self-host, or use one of the commercial OSM hosts, which are still typically far cheaper than the proprietary alternatives.
ODbL versus CC0

OpenStreetMap is share-alike: if you build a derived database and distribute it, that derived database has to carry the same licence. Using OSM to draw a map in your product is fine and normal. Merging OSM into a proprietary dataset you then sell is where you need legal advice.

listings.name: data.gov
listings.limits: None; some agency APIs ask for a free key
listings.realcost: Nothing. It's published by the US government and mostly public domain.
free_includes: Hundreds of thousands of federal, state and local datasets
Census, weather, health, transport, energy and spending data
A free api.data.gov key covering many agency APIs
US federal works are generally public domain — no licence fee, no attribution requirement
listings.short: Yes. It's the US government's own data catalogue — free to download, free to use commercially, and mostly public domain because taxpayers already paid for it.
listings.catch: No price catch. The catch is condition: it's a catalogue pointing at hundreds of agencies, so formats are inconsistent, some links rot, and 'available' doesn't always mean 'clean'.
listings.worth: Commercial vendors repackage this exact data and charge subscriptions for it.
smart_moves: Get one api.data.gov key — it works across many agencies instead of one per API
Go to the agency directly for anything you'll rely on; the catalogue entry can lag the source
Check the update cadence before building on a dataset — some are live, some were published once in 2019
listings.get_summary: In practice: an enormous, free, legally unencumbered dataset library — if you're willing to do the cleaning.
drawbacks: Wildly inconsistent formats and documentation between agencies
Dead links and stale datasets are common
Mostly US-focused
more_info: Public domain is the quiet superpower

Works of the US federal government generally carry no copyright, which means no licence, no attribution clause, and nothing to negotiate before putting the data in a commercial product. Very little other data comes this unencumbered — check the specific dataset, since state, local and contractor-produced data can differ.
Treat the catalogue as an index, not a source

data.gov catalogues what agencies publish; it doesn't host or maintain most of it. For anything going into production, find the agency's own endpoint and subscribe to its update notices, so a schema change doesn't quietly break you.

listings.name: OpenAlex
listings.limits: Generous rate limits; add your email for the polite pool
listings.realcost: Nothing. Nonprofit-run, CC0 licensed, with the full dataset downloadable.
free_includes: Metadata for hundreds of millions of scholarly works, authors and institutions
A full REST API with no key required
The complete dataset as a downloadable snapshot
CC0 licensing — no restrictions on reuse
paid_locked: Premium support and higher-throughput access for institutions
listings.short: Yes. An open replacement for the paid scholarly databases — full API, no key, no account, and the entire dataset downloadable under CC0.
listings.catch: None on price. Metadata coverage is broad but imperfect, and it indexes records rather than hosting the papers themselves.
listings.worth: The commercial equivalents (Scopus, Web of Science) are institutional subscriptions costing tens of thousands a year.
smart_moves: Put your email in the API call to land in the faster 'polite pool' — it's free and it helps them contact you if you misbehave
Take the snapshot for bulk work rather than paginating the API for days
Cross-check against Crossref for anything where a single record matters
listings.get_summary: In practice: the scholarly-metadata layer that used to require a university library subscription.
drawbacks: Metadata quality varies, especially author disambiguation
Indexes metadata, not full text
Younger and less curated than the paid incumbents
more_info: It exists because the old one was bought

OpenAlex was built after Microsoft Academic Graph was discontinued, on the view that the scholarly record shouldn't depend on one company's product roadmap. That origin is the argument for using it: it's structured to be forkable, because the data is CC0 and downloadable in full.

listings.name: Common Crawl
listings.limits: None from Common Crawl; your own storage and egress are the limit
listings.realcost: Nothing to access. Processing petabytes is where your money goes.
free_includes: Petabytes of crawled web pages, updated monthly
Raw pages, extracted text and metadata indexes
Free access from public cloud storage
No licence fee and no usage agreement to sign
paid_locked: Nothing — but compute to process it is on you
listings.short: Yes, the archive is genuinely free. What isn't free is the compute and bandwidth to do anything with several petabytes of it.
listings.catch: The download costs nothing and the processing costs plenty. Pulling a full monthly crawl out of cloud storage can generate a serious egress bill — with the wrong setup that's a four-figure surprise.
listings.worth: The raw material behind a great many search and AI products, given away by a nonprofit.
smart_moves: Use the URL index to fetch only the pages you want instead of downloading crawls whole
Run your processing in the same cloud region as the data so egress stays near zero
Start with the extracted-text files rather than raw WARC unless you need the HTML
listings.get_summary: In practice: a free, enormous snapshot of the public web — for people who already know how to handle data at that scale.
drawbacks: Scale makes casual use impractical
Careless egress can cost real money — the data is free, moving it isn't
Crawl coverage is broad but not complete
more_info: The free thing that can still generate a bill

This is the clearest example on the site of free data with an expensive shadow. Common Crawl charges nothing. Your cloud provider charges for every byte leaving its network. Process in-region, filter with the index first, and the bill stays near zero — do it naively and it won't.

listings.name: Hugging Face Datasets
listings.limits: Fair-use bandwidth; private storage and compute are paid
listings.realcost: An account for some downloads. The hosting is subsidised by the paid business.
free_includes: Hundreds of thousands of public datasets, downloadable
Free hosting for your own public datasets
A streaming loader so you needn't download everything
Dataset cards documenting licence and provenance
paid_locked: Private repositories beyond the free allowance
listings.short: Yes for using and publishing public datasets — that part is free and has stayed free. The paid business is compute and private storage, not access.
listings.catch: Free hosting is subject to fair use, and 'fair use' is defined by the company, not by a published number. Also: the platform is free, but each dataset carries its own licence, and plenty are non-commercial.
listings.worth: Free CDN-backed hosting for large datasets, which would otherwise be a real storage bill.
smart_moves: Read the dataset card's licence before commercial use — the platform being free says nothing about the data
Use streaming mode for large datasets instead of downloading the whole thing
Keep a copy of anything critical; a dataset repo can be taken down by its owner
listings.get_summary: In practice: the default place to find, download and publish machine-learning datasets, free.
drawbacks: Fair-use limits aren't published as hard numbers
Dataset licences vary enormously and some are restrictive
Datasets can disappear when their owner removes them
more_info: The platform's licence is not the data's licence

This trips people constantly. Hugging Face being free to use tells you nothing about whether a given dataset may be used commercially — that is set by whoever uploaded it, on the dataset card. Non-commercial and research-only terms are common. Check per dataset, every time.

listings.name: Open-Meteo
listings.limits: Free for non-commercial use under a daily call allowance
listings.realcost: Nothing for personal and non-commercial projects. Commercial use is a paid plan.
free_includes: Weather forecasts and historical data with no API key at all
Global coverage from national weather-service models
Historical reanalysis going back decades
Open-source code and open data licensing
paid_locked: Higher call volumes and guaranteed uptime
listings.short: Yes for non-commercial use, and unusually so — there is no API key, no signup and no card. You call the URL and get weather back.
listings.catch: The free tier is non-commercial. If it's inside a product you make money from, you're on a paid plan — that boundary is stated plainly rather than hidden, which is more than the incumbent manages.
listings.worth: The main alternative gates comparable data behind an account, a key, and a card on file.
smart_moves: No key means you can test it from a browser address bar in ten seconds
Cache responses — the daily allowance is generous but not infinite
If the project starts earning, move to the commercial plan; the terms are clear
listings.get_summary: In practice: weather data with the lowest barrier to entry of anything in this category.
drawbacks: Non-commercial only on the free tier
No uptime guarantee without a paid plan
Smaller operation than the incumbents
more_info: Why 'no API key' is worth noticing

Requiring a key isn't a technical necessity; it's the hook that attaches your usage to an account, and eventually to a card. A service that answers without one has given up that hook deliberately. It's the clearest signal in this category that the free tier is meant to be used rather than converted.

listings.name: Supabase
listings.limits: 2 active projects; 500MB database; pauses after a week idle
listings.realcost: An account, and the pausing rule. No card for the free plan.
free_includes: A real hosted Postgres database with an auto-generated API
Authentication, file storage and realtime subscriptions
Unlimited API requests
Two active projects at once
paid_locked: Databases beyond the free size and no idle pausing
Daily backups, log retention and support
listings.short: Yes — a genuinely usable free tier with a real Postgres database, no card required. The limits that matter are two active projects and a pause after a week of inactivity.
listings.catch: Free projects pause after about a week with no activity. Nothing is deleted and you can wake it up, but a side project you visit monthly will greet you asleep — and so will your users.
listings.worth: A managed Postgres instance with auth and storage is otherwise $15–25/month at the low end.
smart_moves: Anything with real users needs the paid tier — the pause rule alone makes free unsuitable for production
Two active projects is the real ceiling; archive rather than accumulate
Take your own backups on free — daily backups are a paid feature
listings.get_summary: In practice: a full backend for prototypes and small tools, free, provided nothing depends on it being awake.
drawbacks: Idle projects pause, which rules out low-traffic production use
Only two active projects
No automatic backups on the free plan
more_info: The pause rule, plainly

A week without activity and the project suspends. You can restore it from the dashboard and the data is intact, but the first visitor after a quiet week meets an error rather than your app. For learning, prototyping and internal tools that's fine. For anything a stranger might load, it isn't.

listings.name: Firebase
listings.card: Not for Spark; required for Blaze
listings.autobill: Yes on Blaze — usage-based, no hard cap by default
listings.limits: Spark plan quotas; several services need the paid plan at all
listings.realcost: Free until you need a feature Spark doesn't carry — then it's metered billing.
free_includes: The Spark plan: a hosted database, authentication and hosting at small scale
Generous free quotas for a prototype or small app
No card required to stay on Spark
paid_locked: Cloud Functions and several other services require the Blaze plan
Any usage above the Spark quotas
listings.short: Free to start and genuinely usable at small scale — but the moment you need cloud functions or outgrow the quotas, you move to metered billing with a card attached.
listings.catch: The real risk isn't the upgrade, it's what the upgrade means: Blaze bills by usage with no hard spending cap by default. A loop in your code or a burst of traffic bills you for it, and the budget alert tells you afterwards.
listings.worth: The free quotas genuinely cover a prototype. The danger is the shape of the plan above them.
smart_moves: Set a budget alert the same hour you enable Blaze — before you write any code against it
Alerts notify; they don't stop spend. If a hard ceiling matters, add a function that disables billing when the budget trips
Supabase's free tier covers a lot of the same ground without metered billing at all
listings.get_summary: In practice: a strong free prototype tier attached to a pay-as-you-go plan that has no brakes fitted as standard.
drawbacks: Blaze bills by usage with no default hard cap
Core features like functions aren't available on the free plan at all
Deep lock-in — moving off Firebase later is a rewrite
more_info: Budget alerts are not spending limits

This is the single most important thing to understand before enabling Blaze. A budget in Google Cloud sends a notification when you cross a threshold — it does not stop the meter. Capping spend for real requires wiring the alert to something that actually disables billing. Plenty of people have learned this from an invoice.
Lock-in is the other price

Firebase's database and auth aren't standards you can pick up and move. That is fine while you're small and it is the reason migrations off it are projects rather than afternoons. Weigh that at the start, when switching is still cheap.

listings.name: Google Maps Platform
listings.card: Yes — a billing account is required for a key
listings.autobill: Yes — pay-as-you-go above the free caps
listings.limits: Per-service monthly free caps, replacing the old flat credit
listings.realcost: A card on file from day one, and a bill the month your traffic grows.
free_includes: A monthly free allowance per service — commonly 10,000 calls on the core APIs
Some services, including embedded maps, free without a cap
The full API surface while you're inside the allowance
paid_locked: Everything above each service's monthly free cap
listings.short: Free up to a monthly allowance per service — but you attach a card before you get a key, and everything past the allowance bills automatically.
listings.catch: The structure changed in 2025: the old single monthly credit became a per-service free cap. Nobody is deceiving you, but 'free tier' here means a metered account with a card attached, not a free product.
listings.worth: Real value inside the caps. The reason this listing exists is what happens outside them.
smart_moves: Set API restrictions on the key immediately — an unrestricted key found in your frontend gets used by strangers, and billed to you
Set quota limits per API in the console; those are hard caps, unlike budget alerts
For a static map or a handful of lookups, OpenStreetMap does it with no card at all
listings.get_summary: In practice: excellent data, metered from the first day, with the free allowance as the on-ramp.
drawbacks: A billing account with a card is required before you can start
Overages bill automatically
A leaked or unrestricted key is billed to you, not the person using it
more_info: Restrict the key on day one

Maps keys live in frontend code where anyone can read them. An unrestricted key can be lifted and used by strangers against your billing account. Restrict by HTTP referrer or IP and by API, and set per-API quota caps — those are real ceilings, where a budget alert is only a message.
What changed in 2025

The long-standing flat monthly credit was replaced with per-service free caps. For small users the practical result is broadly similar; for anyone modelling costs, the arithmetic is different, so recalculate against the current SKU table rather than the figure you remember.

listings.name: Reddit API
listings.account: Reddit account and registered app required
listings.limits: Rate-limited free access for non-commercial use; commercial access is priced
listings.realcost: Free for small non-commercial use. Commercial or high-volume access is a negotiated bill.
free_includes: Rate-limited API access for non-commercial projects
Reading public posts and comments
Building personal tools and research scripts
paid_locked: Anything at the scale a real app needs
listings.short: Free for small, non-commercial use under rate limits. Commercial and high-volume access is priced — which is what ended the third-party app ecosystem in 2023.
listings.catch: This is the site's thesis with a body count. The API was effectively free for years, third-party apps were built on it, and 2023 pricing shut them down within weeks. The free tier that remains is real, but it is sized for hobbies, not products.
listings.worth: Still genuinely useful for research and personal tools. Not a foundation to build a business on.
smart_moves: Fine for a personal script or a research project — that's what the free tier is for
Don't architect anything commercial around it without pricing the commercial tier first
Cache aggressively; the rate limits are the binding constraint long before anything else
listings.get_summary: In practice: a usable free tier for personal and research work, on a platform that has already demonstrated it will reprice.
drawbacks: Commercial use requires paid access
Rate limits make real applications impractical on free
A demonstrated history of changing terms with little notice
more_info: What 2023 actually proved

Apollo, Reddit is Fun and others were long-established apps with paying users. New API pricing made them unviable and they shut down within weeks. Nothing about it was illegal or even hidden — which is the point. A free tier is a business decision that can be reversed, and building on one without a migration plan is a bet on someone else's roadmap.

listings.name: X (Twitter) API
listings.limits: No free tier for new developers
listings.realcost: Metered from the first call. The old free tier is closed to new signups.
free_includes: Nothing for new developers
listings.short: No. The free tier is closed to new developers — X moved to pay-per-use in February 2026, so access is metered from your first call.
listings.catch: There's no deception, just a closed door. What makes it worth a listing is the trajectory: a famously open free API became $100/month, then $200, then tiers, then metered — inside three years. People still arrive expecting the old one.
listings.worth: Nothing at zero. Price it as a paid data source or use something else.
smart_moves: If a tutorial shows a free tier, check its date — anything before 2026 describes a product that no longer exists
Academic access has been repeatedly restricted; don't assume a research exemption
For social data generally, Reddit's free tier and Mastodon's open API are what remain
listings.get_summary: In practice: a paid data product. Budget for it or design around it.
drawbacks: No free tier for new developers
Pricing has changed repeatedly and abruptly
Existing subscribers have been migrated to metered billing
more_info: The clearest free-tier death in tech

Until 2023 the API was free enough that an entire ecosystem of clients, research projects and bots ran on it. Then free access ended, paid tiers appeared and were repriced more than once, and in February 2026 the tiers themselves gave way to pay-per-use with no free option for new developers. If you want one example of why this site puts a date on every verdict, it is this one.

listings.name: IRS Free File
listings.limits: Income cap — 2025 adjusted gross income of $89,000 or less
listings.realcost: Nothing for federal filing if you're under the cap. State returns vary by provider.
free_includes: Guided federal tax preparation and e-filing, free
Real commercial tax software, provided through the IRS partnership
Free state returns from some providers
Fillable Forms for any income, if you're happy doing it yourself
listings.short: Yes, genuinely — if your income qualifies. IRS Free File is a partnership between the IRS and tax software companies giving free federal filing to taxpayers under the income cap. It is the answer to every listing on this site that advertises free filing and then charges mid-return.
listings.catch: Two real ones. The cap is on adjusted gross income and it moves each year, so check before assuming. And you must enter through the IRS site — going to the same company directly lands you in their commercial product, where the free version has much narrower rules. That single click is the entire difference.
listings.worth: $40–130, which is what the same return costs once a commercial product decides your situation isn't simple.
smart_moves: Always start at irs.gov/freefile, never at the provider's own site — the free tier there is a different, stingier product
Compare providers inside the tool: state returns are free with some and charged by others
Over the cap? Free Fillable Forms has no income limit — no hand-holding, but no bill either
IRS Direct File, the government's own filing tool, is not available for the 2026 season
listings.get_summary: In practice: the free federal filing that the advertised free filing keeps failing to be.
drawbacks: Income cap excludes higher earners from the guided software
State filing isn't free with every provider
The entry point matters — arriving via the company's own site loses the offer
more_info: Why the entry point decides whether it's free

Free File providers run two products: the IRS-partnership version with generous eligibility, and their own commercial 'free edition' with narrow rules that pushes upgrades. They look similar. Entering through irs.gov is what puts you in the first one, and it is the most valuable click in this entire category.
What happened to Direct File

The IRS built its own free filing tool, piloted it in 2024 and expanded it to 25 states in 2025. It was discontinued ahead of the 2026 filing season with no relaunch date. Free File, the older public-private partnership, is unaffected and still running — which is why this listing points there.

listings.name: Jellyfin
listings.account: Local only, on your own server
listings.limits: None imposed by anyone — your hardware is the limit
listings.realcost: Nothing. Volunteer-run, open source, no company behind it.
free_includes: A full media server for your own films, shows and music
Remote streaming from anywhere — no pass, no subscription
Apps for phones, tablets, TVs and consoles
Live TV and DVR with a tuner, hardware transcoding included
listings.short: Yes, entirely. Jellyfin is a free, open-source media server with no paid tier, no account with a company, and nothing gated — including the remote streaming that Plex started charging for in 2025.
listings.catch: The catch is effort, not money. You set it up yourself, and reaching it from outside your home means dealing with your own network. Nobody is on call when it breaks.
listings.worth: Directly replaces a Plex Pass or Remote Watch Pass, and the hardware transcoding that sits behind Plex's paywall is simply included.
smart_moves: This is the answer to Plex's 2025 change: remote playback of your own files, with nothing to pay
Use Tailscale or a VPN for remote access rather than opening ports — easier and safer
Its clients are less polished than Plex's; try one on your TV before migrating a big library
listings.get_summary: In practice: everything Plex does with your own media, minus the subscription that arrived in 2025.
drawbacks: Setup and maintenance are yours
TV apps are rougher than Plex's
No official support — community forums only
more_info: Why it exists

Jellyfin was forked from Emby when that project moved to a proprietary licence. It is run by volunteers with no company, no funding round and nothing to monetise later — which is the structural reason it cannot do what Plex did in 2025. There is no one to decide that remote streaming should now cost money.

listings.name: Anki
listings.limits: Free on desktop and Android; the iPhone and iPad app is paid
listings.realcost: Nothing, unless you want it on an iPhone — that app is a one-off $24.99.
free_includes: The full desktop app on Windows, macOS and Linux
AnkiDroid on Android, free and full-featured
AnkiWeb sync across devices, free
Every shared deck, and unlimited cards
paid_locked: AnkiMobile for iPhone and iPad — a one-time purchase, not a subscription
listings.short: Free on desktop, Android and the web, with unlimited cards and free syncing. The one exception is iOS, where the official app costs a one-off $24.99 — and that purchase funds the whole project.
listings.catch: The catch is one platform. Everything is free except the iPhone app, and there is no free official iOS client. It's a one-time payment rather than a subscription, and it is what pays for the free versions everyone else uses.
listings.worth: Paid flashcard apps run $5–15/month. Anki is $0 forever on most platforms, or $24.99 once on iOS.
smart_moves: On Android, AnkiDroid is free and does everything — no reason to pay anything
iPhone users can study free at ankiweb.net in the browser rather than buying the app
Download shared decks before building your own; the medical and language decks are enormous
listings.get_summary: In practice: the spaced-repetition tool serious learners use, free everywhere except one platform.
drawbacks: The interface is dated and the options are overwhelming at first
No free official iOS app
Shared decks vary wildly in quality
more_info: An honest paid app

It is worth naming what this is not. There is no subscription, no upsell inside the free versions, no ads, and no feature held hostage. One platform's app costs money once, and it funds development for everyone else. Compared with almost everything else on this site, that is a straightforward arrangement.

listings.name: Internet Archive
listings.limits: Lending is limited per title; everything else is open
listings.realcost: Nothing. A nonprofit library funded by donations and grants.
free_includes: Millions of public-domain books, films, concerts and recordings
The Wayback Machine — the web as it used to be
Free borrowing of scanned books, with waits
Software, radio and TV archives you cannot get anywhere else
listings.short: Yes. A nonprofit digital library with no paid tier — millions of public-domain works, the Wayback Machine, and a lending library of scanned books. Free to use and free to search.
listings.catch: No catch on price. The uncertainty is legal: publishers won their case against the Archive's lending programme, so what is borrowable has narrowed and may narrow further. Public-domain material and the Wayback Machine are unaffected.
listings.worth: Irreplaceable rather than merely cheap — much of what it holds exists nowhere else.
smart_moves: The Wayback Machine settles arguments: it shows what a page said before it was quietly edited
Public-domain texts here have no lending limits at all — only in-copyright scans do
Donate if you use it heavily; it runs on donations and it is the memory of the web
listings.get_summary: In practice: a library, an archive of the web, and a media collection — none of it charged for.
drawbacks: Scan quality varies enormously
The lending catalogue has thinned after litigation
Search and navigation are functional rather than pleasant
more_info: Its most underused feature

The Wayback Machine is the reason this site can prove what a company's pricing page said last year. If you ever need to show that a free tier existed before it quietly disappeared, that is where the evidence lives.

listings.name: Ollama
listings.limits: Your own hardware — RAM decides which models you can run
listings.realcost: Nothing. Open source, and the models are downloaded, not rented.
free_includes: Run open-weight models locally with one command
No usage caps, no message limits, no queue
Fully offline once a model is downloaded
An API on your own machine for building against
paid_locked: Nothing — hosted services sell convenience, not capability
listings.short: Yes, completely. Ollama runs open-weight AI models on your own computer: no account, no key, no cap, and nothing leaves your machine.
listings.catch: The catch is hardware. Small models run on an ordinary laptop; the good ones want serious RAM and a decent GPU, and without them you'll get slow answers from a weaker model than the free hosted chatbots give you.
listings.worth: Unlimited private inference against $20/month subscriptions — provided your machine can keep up.
smart_moves: Start with a small model to check your hardware before downloading a 40GB one
This is the only entry in this category where your conversations genuinely never leave your computer
Pair it with an open-weight model from Hugging Face; the weights and the runner are both free
listings.get_summary: In practice: unlimited, private, offline AI — bounded by your hardware rather than by anyone's plan.
drawbacks: Needs real RAM and ideally a GPU
Local models lag the best hosted ones
Command-line first; the polish isn't there
more_info: The only free tier nobody can withdraw

Every other listing in this category is someone's free tier, which means someone can change it — and this site exists because they do. A model on your own disk cannot be rate-limited, repriced or discontinued. That is a different kind of free from all the rest.

listings.name: VSCodium
listings.limits: None
listings.realcost: Nothing. Community builds of Microsoft's own open-source code.
free_includes: The VS Code editor, built from source without Microsoft's telemetry
Every language and extension workflow developers expect
Builds for Windows, macOS and Linux
No account prompts and no branding
listings.short: Yes. VSCodium is VS Code compiled from the same open-source repository with Microsoft's telemetry and branding removed. Same editor, no tracking, no account.
listings.catch: One practical wrinkle: it uses a different extension marketplace, because Microsoft's is licensed for their own builds only. Most extensions are there; a few Microsoft-published ones aren't.
listings.worth: The same as VS Code — which is to say free — with the telemetry difference being the entire point.
smart_moves: Pick this over VS Code if the default telemetry is the thing that bothers you
Check your must-have extensions in the Open VSX registry before switching
Settings and keybindings transfer straight across from VS Code
listings.get_summary: In practice: the same editor most developers already use, with the data collection compiled out.
drawbacks: A different extension marketplace with some gaps
Some Microsoft extensions are licensed against use here
Updates trail the official builds slightly
more_info: What the difference actually is

VS Code's source is open, but the build Microsoft ships adds telemetry, their marketplace and a proprietary licence. VSCodium is the same source compiled without those. If you are happy with VS Code, nothing here is an upgrade — it only matters if you would rather not send usage data to Microsoft.

listings.name: WordPress.org (self-hosted)
listings.limits: None on the software — you supply the hosting
listings.realcost: The software is free. Hosting and a domain are not, and that is the whole difference from WordPress.com.
free_includes: The complete WordPress software, GPLv2, free to download
Every plugin and theme, including commercial use of the software itself
No ads on your site, ever, and no platform branding
Your own database and files — you can move hosts or leave entirely
paid_locked: Nothing in the software. Hosting, a domain and premium plugins are separate purchases.
listings.short: Yes — the software itself is free, and always has been. WordPress.org is the GPL-licensed application that powers a large share of the web. What costs money is hosting it: a server and a domain, typically a few dollars a month from any host.
listings.catch: The catch is that “free software” and “free website” are different things, and this is the confusion the whole WordPress question rests on. Nobody charges you for WordPress. Somebody will charge you to run it. Budget for hosting, a domain, and the hours to maintain updates and backups yourself.
listings.worth: A site with no platform ads, no subdomain and no plugin restrictions — the things WordPress.com charges to remove — for the price of hosting alone.
smart_moves: This is the answer to “is WordPress free” for most people: the software is, the hosting isn't
Many hosts offer one-click installs, so you never touch the download
You own the database — exporting and moving hosts is a real option, unlike hosted builders
Wanting zero cost with zero setup? That is WordPress.com's free plan, with its ads and subdomain
listings.get_summary: In practice: free, unrestricted website software that you pay someone else to run.
drawbacks: Hosting and a domain are real recurring costs
Updates, backups and security are your responsibility
The plugin ecosystem is where paid upsells live
more_info: WordPress.org vs WordPress.com, plainly

They share a name and almost nothing else. WordPress.org is the free software you install anywhere; WordPress.com is a hosted service from Automattic that runs that software for you and sells plans. If you searched “is WordPress free” and got a confusing answer, this is why: one is free and needs hosting, the other is hosted and needs a plan for anything serious.
What GPLv2 actually gives you

The licence lets you use, modify and redistribute the software, including commercially. It is the reason no one can revoke your copy or start charging you for it — a guarantee no hosted free tier on this site can make.

free_alternatives.name: WordPress.com
free_alternatives.why: Hosted for you at no cost, if you accept its ads and subdomain

deals.name: Canva Pro
deals.summary: Verified K-12 teachers and registered nonprofits get Canva Pro — the full $120/year product — completely free through Canva for Education and Canva for Nonprofits.
deals.who: K-12 teachers (verified via school email), registered nonprofits
deals.how: Apply at canva.com/education or canva.com/canva-for-nonprofits with verification
deals.worth: ~$120/year — the full Pro plan with premium assets, background remover, brand kits, and 100GB storage
deals.caveat: Requires verification; processing takes a few days. The education program covers teachers and classrooms, not individual students.

deals.name: GitHub Education
deals.summary: Verified students get GitHub Pro free plus a bundle of developer tools, cloud credits, and domains — the Student Developer Pack — worth thousands in aggregate.
deals.who: Students 13+ at accredited institutions
deals.how: Apply at education.github.com with a school email or enrollment proof
deals.worth: GitHub Pro ($4/month) plus partner credits from cloud providers, domain registrars, and dev tools — collectively $1,000+ in first-year value
deals.caveat: Requires re-verification annually. Individual partner offers have their own terms and expiry windows.

deals.name: Figma Education
deals.summary: Verified students and educators get Figma's Professional plan — normally $12–20/user/month — free for up to two years.
deals.who: Students and educators at accredited institutions
deals.how: Apply at figma.com/education with school email verification
deals.worth: ~$144–240/year — unlimited files, team libraries, and full version history
deals.caveat: Lasts up to two years; must re-verify. Graduates lose access when student status ends.

deals.name: Notion for Education
deals.summary: Students and educators with a school email get Notion's Plus plan free — the same tier that costs individuals $10/month.
deals.who: Students and teachers with a .edu or equivalent school email
deals.how: Sign up with your school email; the upgrade applies automatically
deals.worth: ~$96/year — unlimited blocks for teams, 30-day version history, and unlimited file uploads
deals.caveat: Automatic via school email domain; no application form needed. Access lasts while the school email is active.

deals.name: Apple Music Student
deals.summary: Verified students get Apple Music at roughly half price — plus Apple TV+ included free for the duration of the student subscription.
deals.who: Students enrolled at eligible institutions (verified via UNiDAYS)
deals.how: Subscribe through Apple Music and verify student status via UNiDAYS
deals.worth: ~$6/month savings plus free Apple TV+ (normally $10/month) — roughly $190/year in total value
deals.caveat: Re-verification required periodically. Maxes out at 48 months total.

deals.name: Spotify Student
deals.summary: Verified students get Spotify Premium at a discount, often bundled with Hulu (ad-supported) and Showtime in the US.
deals.who: Students enrolled at accredited US institutions
deals.how: Subscribe at spotify.com/student and verify via SheerID
deals.worth: Premium plus streaming services at a fraction of buying each separately
deals.caveat: Re-verification every 12 months; limit of 4 years total. Bundle components and pricing change by region.

deals.name: JetBrains Student
deals.summary: Verified students and teachers get every JetBrains IDE — IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm, the full suite — free for the duration of their studies.
deals.who: Students and teachers at accredited institutions
deals.how: Apply at jetbrains.com/community/education with school email, ISIC card, or official document
deals.worth: The All Products Pack runs $289/year at full price — every IDE, free
deals.caveat: For non-commercial, educational use only. Annual renewal with re-verification required.

deals.name: LinkedIn Learning via Library
deals.summary: Many public libraries include full LinkedIn Learning access — the same ~$30/month product — free with a library card, no trial, no credit card, no expiry.
deals.who: Anyone with a card at a participating public library
deals.how: Visit your library's website, look under digital resources or databases for LinkedIn Learning
deals.worth: ~$360/year — the full course library with certificates that post to your LinkedIn profile
deals.caveat: Not every library participates; check yours first. Access is via the library portal, not linkedin.com directly.

deals.name: Adobe Creative Cloud Student
deals.summary: Verified students and teachers get the full Creative Cloud suite at roughly 60% off the standard price for the first year.
deals.who: Students 13+ and teachers at accredited institutions
deals.how: Purchase through adobe.com/creativecloud/plans with student verification
deals.worth: Saves roughly $420 in the first year versus the standard All Apps price
deals.caveat: First-year pricing jumps to a higher (still discounted) rate at renewal — read the renewal price before committing. The annual plan's early-termination fee still applies.

deals.name: Audible 3-month trial (seasonal)
deals.summary: Audible periodically offers 3-month free trials (vs. the standard 30-day) during Prime Day, holidays, and promotional events. Three credits instead of one — and all books claimed stay yours.
deals.who: New Audible subscribers (sometimes returning subscribers after a gap)
deals.how: Watch for the offer during Prime Day (July), Black Friday, and holiday sales; the landing page changes
deals.worth: 3 premium audiobooks ($45–75 retail value) kept forever, even after cancelling
deals.caveat: Seasonal and unpredictable; the standard offer is 1 month / 1 credit. Same auto-billing mechanics apply — alarm the end date regardless of trial length.

deals.name: NordVPN / Surfshark / ExpressVPN sales
deals.summary: The major VPN providers perpetually advertise 70–85% off, but the discount applies only to 2-year prepaid plans — the monthly rate after that period reverts to full price unless you cancel.
deals.who: Anyone — these are the standard offers, not special promotions
deals.how: Visit any VPN provider's homepage; the 'sale' is always running
deals.worth: Real savings vs. monthly billing — but only for the prepaid term. The headline rate is the commitment price, not the renewal price.
deals.caveat: The '83% off' is real math but misleading framing: you're comparing a 2-year prepaid rate to a monthly rate nobody pays. Read the renewal price before committing, and calendar the renewal date — VPN auto-renewals at full price are one of the most common surprise charges online.

deals.name: Costco membership cashback
deals.summary: Costco's membership comes with an unconditional satisfaction guarantee: cancel at any time for a full refund of your membership fee, no questions asked.
deals.who: Anyone considering or holding a Costco membership
deals.how: Cancel at any membership desk or through your online account
deals.worth: The entire membership fee back — the 'risk-free trial' that's actually risk-free because no card trap exists. The Executive membership additionally earns 2% back on purchases.
deals.caveat: Refunding after using the membership all year is technically allowed but tests the spirit of the policy. The Executive tier's 2% reward is capped annually.

deals.name: SCORE Business Mentoring
deals.type: Free ongoing business mentoring — truly free
deals.summary: 10,000 volunteer business mentors, backed by the U.S. Small Business Administration, offering free one-on-one advising by phone, video, email, or in person. Not a single session — for the life of your business. No catch, no upsell, no fee.
deals.who: Anyone in the US with a business idea, a startup, or an existing business at any stage
deals.how: Enter your zip code at score.org/find-mentor, fill out a request form, and get matched with a mentor in your industry
deals.worth: Business consulting runs $150–400/hour. SCORE mentors provide ongoing guidance — the equivalent of thousands in advisory fees, free, indefinitely.
deals.caveat: Mentor quality varies — they're volunteers with real experience, but expertise ranges. You can request a different mentor at any time. US-based businesses only.

deals.name: SBA Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs)
deals.summary: Nearly 1,000 SBDC locations nationwide offering free, confidential one-on-one business consulting on planning, financing, marketing, management, and operations. Funded by the SBA and hosted at universities and colleges.
deals.who: Any current or aspiring small business owner in the US
deals.how: Find your local SBDC at sba.gov and schedule an appointment — virtual or in-person
deals.worth: Professional business consulting at $0, covering areas where private consultants charge $100–300/hour. Advisors have real industry and academic credentials.
deals.caveat: Availability varies by location and demand. Sessions focus on advising, not doing the work for you. Some locations have waiting lists during peak times.

deals.name: ABA Free Legal Answers
deals.type: Free legal advice from volunteer attorneys
deals.summary: The American Bar Association's pro bono portal where income-eligible individuals submit civil legal questions online and receive written answers from volunteer attorneys licensed in their state. Nearly 500,000 questions answered to date.
deals.who: Income-eligible individuals in the US with civil (non-criminal) legal questions
deals.how: Create an account at abafreelegalanswers.org, verify income eligibility, and submit your legal question
deals.worth: A single hour of legal advice runs $200–500+. This provides targeted written guidance from a licensed attorney at $0.
deals.caveat: Civil questions only — no criminal, immigration (separate federal portal exists), or ongoing representation. Answers are brief legal guidance, not full legal representation. Income eligibility requirements apply.

deals.name: VITA Free Tax Preparation
deals.type: Free in-person tax filing by IRS-certified volunteers
deals.summary: The IRS Volunteer Income Tax Assistance program provides free tax preparation by certified volunteers at community locations nationwide — for people who earn roughly $67,000 or less, have disabilities, or have limited English. A real human prepares and files your return at $0.
deals.who: Individuals and families earning approximately $67,000 or less, people with disabilities, and limited-English speakers
deals.how: Find a VITA site near you using the IRS locator tool at irs.gov or by calling 800-906-9887
deals.worth: Tax preparation fees run $150–500+ depending on complexity. VITA covers the same service at $0, done by a trained, IRS-certified human.
deals.caveat: Seasonal — operates January through mid-April at most sites. Some locations serve year-round. Bring all tax documents. Wait times can be long during peak season.

deals.name: Apple Store Free Sessions (Today at Apple)
deals.type: Free creative workshops and one-on-one help
deals.summary: Every Apple Store offers free daily sessions: creative workshops on photography, music, video, design, and coding, plus free one-on-one personal setup and troubleshooting for any Apple product — no purchase required for the workshops.
deals.who: Anyone — no Apple purchase required for workshop attendance
deals.how: Browse and register at apple.com/today or walk into any Apple Store
deals.worth: Creative workshops and tech support at $0 in a beautifully designed space. Private tutoring in these subjects runs $50–100/hour.
deals.caveat: Workshops teach Apple's ecosystem (iPhone photography, GarageBand, etc.) — genuine education, but inside Apple's world. One-on-one Genius Bar support for repairs may lead to paid service recommendations.

deals.name: HubSpot Free Business Courses & Certifications
deals.type: Free marketing, sales, and business certifications
deals.summary: HubSpot Academy offers free courses and industry-recognized certifications in digital marketing, content strategy, sales, SEO, and CRM — taught by real practitioners, with no card and no trial clock.
deals.who: Anyone — no HubSpot product purchase required
deals.how: Create a free HubSpot Academy account and start any course or certification track
deals.worth: Comparable marketing certifications from other providers run $200–500. HubSpot's are free and genuinely respected in the industry.
deals.caveat: The courses naturally feature HubSpot's own tools — genuine education inside their ecosystem. Certifications require periodic renewal. The knowledge transfers; the tool-specific parts are the upsell.

deals.name: Shopify Free Business Courses (Shopify Learn)
deals.summary: Shopify Learn offers free courses on starting an online business, product photography, social media marketing, and e-commerce fundamentals — no Shopify subscription required to take them.
deals.who: Anyone — no Shopify account needed for most courses
deals.how: Browse courses at shopify.com/learn and start watching
deals.worth: E-commerce courses elsewhere run $50–200. These are free and taught by successful Shopify merchants.
deals.caveat: The courses naturally point toward building on Shopify — real education, inside their funnel. The business knowledge transfers regardless of platform.

deals.name: Google for Small Business (free tools & coaching)
deals.type: Free digital skills training and business tools
deals.summary: Google bundles its free small business tools — Business Profile, Analytics, Search Console, and digital skills training — into one portal with personalized recommendations, coaching resources, and free workshops.
deals.who: Any small business owner
deals.how: Visit smallbusiness.withgoogle.com and follow the guided setup for your business type
deals.worth: A digital marketing agency charges thousands to set up what Google gives away for free here — because your business activity on these tools feeds Google's ad ecosystem.
deals.caveat: Every free tool ultimately serves Google's ad business. The tools are genuinely useful; the ecosystem they build is the product. Use them knowingly.

deals.name: DreamSite Design — Free 30-Minute Consultation
deals.summary: A free 30-minute consultation with a DreamSite Design web strategist — site audits, redesign planning, new builds, or just honest answers about what your site needs. No obligation, no pitch timer. Use code VERIFREEDREAM when booking.
deals.who: Any business or individual with a web project or question
deals.how: Visit dreamsitedesign.com and book a consultation using code VERIFREEDREAM
deals.worth: Web design consultations typically run $75–200/half hour. This one is $0 with the code — a genuine front-door offer from the studio.
deals.caveat: The consultation is genuinely free and the code is real; if the studio ever stops honouring it, this listing comes down. The consultation is advice, not deliverables — hired work is quoted separately.
deals.disclosure: DreamSite Design and Verified Free share an owner. Listed on the same rubric as every other deal here.

deals.name: The Library Card Stack
deals.type: One card unlocks ~$800+/year in free services
deals.summary: A single public library card — free to get — unlocks Libby (bestseller ebooks and audiobooks), Hoopla (movies, music, comics), Kanopy (art-house films), and often LinkedIn Learning, PressReader (newspapers), and Ancestry Library Edition. Combined value: $800+ per year in subscriptions replaced.
deals.who: Anyone with a residential address — most libraries issue cards for free to residents
deals.how: Walk into your local public library with ID showing your address. Many now offer instant digital cards online too.
deals.worth: Libby replaces Kindle Unlimited (~$144/yr) and Audible (~$180/yr). Hoopla replaces multiple streaming services. Kanopy replaces art-house subscriptions (~$120/yr). LinkedIn Learning is $360/yr. Total: $800+ in services, all on one free card.
deals.caveat: Not every library carries every service — check your library's digital resources page. Multiple library cards (home, work city, non-resident cards) multiply access. This is the single highest-value free thing in America and almost nobody uses it fully.

deals.name: Walmart+ 30-Day Trial (includes Paramount+ and Peacock)
deals.summary: Walmart+ includes Paramount+ and Peacock as bundled perks. The 30-day free trial of Walmart+ gives you both streaming services plus free delivery, gas discounts, and more — all in one trial.
deals.who: New Walmart+ subscribers (US)
deals.how: Sign up at walmart.com/plus — card required, auto-bills at $12.95/month after 30 days
deals.worth: Paramount+ ($7.99/mo) + Peacock ($10.99/mo) + free delivery + gas savings, all bundled into one $12.95/mo subscription — or free for 30 days during the trial.
deals.caveat: Card required, auto-renews. Same rules as every trial on this site: calendar day 27, cancel on the website, screenshot confirmation. The streaming perks are the ad-supported tiers.

deals.name: Hulu 30-Day Free Trial
deals.type: The longest premium streaming trial still standing
deals.summary: Hulu still offers a full 30-day free trial — the longest among major streamers now that Netflix, Disney+, and Max have dropped theirs. That's enough to binge two or three complete series.
deals.who: New Hulu subscribers (US)
deals.how: Sign up at hulu.com — card required, rolls into $9.99/month with ads after 30 days
deals.worth: A full month of a $10/month service: originals, next-day network TV, and a deep back catalog. Time it around a series premiere for maximum value.
deals.caveat: Card required, auto-bills. The 30-day window is generous — plan your watchlist before starting. Cancel the same day you sign up; Hulu keeps the trial running through the full 30 days.

deals.name: Apple TV+ 3 Months Free (with any new Apple device)
deals.summary: Buy any new iPhone, iPad, Mac, or Apple TV and get three months of Apple TV+ free — the same service that runs $12.99/month normally. Activate within 90 days of device setup.
deals.who: Buyers of any new Apple device
deals.how: Open the Apple TV app on your new device within 90 days of first setup — the offer appears automatically
deals.worth: ~$39 in Apple TV+ access. Quality over quantity: Ted Lasso, Severance, The Morning Show, For All Mankind.
deals.caveat: Auto-renews at $12.99/month after the three months. The offer only appears once per device, and only on the new hardware — not on your old iPhone after buying AirPods. Set the cancellation reminder.

deals.name: Anthropic API $5 Free Credit
deals.type: Free developer credits — no card needed
deals.summary: Every new Anthropic API account gets $5 in free credits — no payment details required. Enough to build a small prototype, run a personal automation, or test Claude in your own code.
deals.who: Developers and builders — anyone who can write or paste code
deals.how: Create an account at console.anthropic.com — credits appear automatically, no card needed
deals.worth: $5 covers roughly 1.5 million tokens on the fastest model or ~300K tokens on the mid-tier — enough for a working prototype.
deals.caveat: Developer-facing — this is API access, not the chat interface (which has its own free tier). Credits expire after a period. Once spent, you add a card to continue.

deals.name: ChatGPT Plus Free for US Military & Veterans
deals.type: One year of ChatGPT Plus — free, verified
deals.summary: Active US military servicemembers and veterans get a full year of ChatGPT Plus ($20/month value) free through SheerID verification. No card required for the free year.
deals.who: US active-duty military, reserves, and veterans
deals.how: Verify military status through SheerID on OpenAI's website
deals.worth: $240/year — the full Plus subscription with priority access, the strongest models, and all premium features.
deals.caveat: One year only; renews at full price afterward unless cancelled. Verification through SheerID — have your military documentation ready.

deals.name: Sling Freestream — Free Live TV
deals.type: Permanently free live TV — no card, no trial
deals.summary: Sling Freestream offers ~100 free live channels — mostly news (ABC News, CBS News, BBC) plus some movies and entertainment — with no account, no card, and no trial clock. Separate from Sling's paid plans.
deals.who: Anyone in the US
deals.how: Visit sling.com/freestream or open the Sling app — no signup required
deals.worth: Free live news and entertainment channels at $0 — add it to your Tubi/Pluto/Roku Channel rotation.
deals.caveat: Heavy on news, light on entertainment compared to Tubi or Pluto TV. The paid Sling plans ($40+/month) are a separate product that includes sports and full cable networks.

deals.name: Amazon Trade-In (gift cards for old devices)
deals.type: Free Amazon credit for old electronics
deals.summary: Amazon accepts old Kindles, Echo devices, tablets, and some electronics in any condition — even broken — and gives you an Amazon gift card plus a discount on a replacement device. Not technically free, but turns e-waste into credit.
deals.who: Anyone with old Amazon devices or eligible electronics
deals.how: Visit amazon.com/trade-in, select your device, get a prepaid shipping label, and send it in
deals.worth: Varies: a working Kindle can return $5–25 in credit; broken devices still earn something. The replacement discount (often 20% off) stacks with the credit.
deals.caveat: Values are low for old or broken devices — this is recycling with a small reward, not a resale market. Gift card credit only, not cash.

deals.name: Costco — Risk-Free 100% Satisfaction Guarantee
deals.summary: Costco refunds almost anything, at almost any time, if you're genuinely not satisfied — no receipt needed, since purchases are tied to your membership. The rare exceptions: electronics carry a 90-day window, and items like tires or batteries fall under product warranties. This is a real safety net for honest buyers, not a loophole to exploit.
deals.who: Costco members (membership itself is also refundable if you're unhappy)
deals.how: Bring the item to any Costco warehouse, or start an online return for Costco.com orders — your membership pulls up the purchase
deals.worth: Genuine protection on big-ticket buys: if an appliance disappoints in month four, you're covered where most retailers would refuse.
deals.caveat: Good-faith policy. Costco does track returns, and abuse (habitual 'used it up, brought it back') can get a membership revoked. It works because most people use it honestly — treat it as a satisfaction guarantee, not free rental.

deals.name: REI — 100% Satisfaction Guarantee (1 Year for Co-op Members)
deals.summary: REI Co-op members get a full year to return most gear if it doesn't perform — you can genuinely test hiking boots or a tent and bring them back if they blister or leak. Non-members get 90 days. Electronics are capped at 90 days for everyone. The one-time $30 lifetime membership pays for itself on a single high-ticket return.
deals.who: Anyone; Co-op members ($30 once, for life) get the full year
deals.how: Return in-store free, or by mail for a $5.99 fee ($21.95 oversize) deducted from your refund. Used gear must be cleaned first or it's rejected.
deals.worth: The year-long window on tested outdoor gear is genuinely rare — real protection against gear that fails on the trail.
deals.caveat: The famous 'lifetime' policy is gone (ended 2013 after abuse). Clean your gear before returning — muddy boots get sent back at your expense. This is for gear that genuinely underperforms, not buyer's remorse on a used season.

deals.name: Zappos — 365-Day Free Returns
deals.type: Full year, free return shipping both ways
deals.summary: Zappos gives you a full 365 days to return unworn shoes for a complete refund, and pays return shipping both ways — a big reason it became the default for buying shoes online, where fit is a gamble. Shoes must be unworn and in the original box with tags (and security tag, if one came attached).
deals.who: Anyone shopping Zappos.com
deals.how: Start a return online within 365 days; Zappos emails a prepaid label and credits your original payment in 5–10 business days
deals.worth: The year window plus free two-way shipping removes the risk from buying shoes you can't try on first.
deals.caveat: Unworn only — try shoes on carpet indoors, not outside. This protects honest 'didn't fit / didn't suit me' returns; wearing them out and returning them is return fraud, which raises prices for everyone. Note the discount outlet (6pm) does NOT share this policy.

deals.name: Target — 90 Days (1 Year on Target-Owned Brands)
deals.summary: Target gives 90 days on most items with a receipt, and a full year on its own brands — Cat & Jack kids' clothing, Good & Gather, Boots & Barkley and others — even after they're worn or washed. RedCard holders get an extra 30 days on the standard window. Cat & Jack's year-long guarantee on worn-through kids' clothes is legitimately generous.
deals.who: Anyone; RedCard holders get +30 days on standard returns
deals.how: Return in-store with receipt (or via Target Circle app / Drive Up at many locations); online orders include free return shipping
deals.worth: The Target-brand year — especially Cat & Jack for kids who destroy clothes — is real, honest value for families.
deals.caveat: The one-year window is for Target-owned brands only, not everything in the store. Keep the receipt or use a tracked account. Designed for genuine wear-and-fail, not wardrobing.

deals.name: Patagonia — Ironclad Guarantee (repair first)
deals.type: Satisfaction guarantee with free repair for wear
deals.summary: Patagonia stands behind everything it makes: if an item doesn't meet your needs, return it for a repair, replacement, or refund. What sets it apart is that normal wear-and-tear damage is repaired — often free or at low cost — rather than tossed, in keeping with the company's reduce-waste mission. It's a guarantee built to extend a product's life, not to churn it.
deals.who: Anyone who buys Patagonia
deals.how: Return unsatisfactory items for refund/replacement; send worn gear to Patagonia's repair service (the largest garment repair operation in North America)
deals.worth: Free or cheap repairs on gear you intend to keep for years — value measured in decades, not a return window.
deals.caveat: This one actively rewards good faith: the ethos is 'keep it longer,' not 'return it faster.' Using the repair service as intended is exactly the point — no misuse angle here, just a company that would rather fix than replace.

comparisons.title: Best Free Image Editors Compared
comparisons.desc: Photopea vs GIMP vs Canva — which free image editor actually fits your workflow? Side-by-side scores, features, and honest picks.
comparisons.intro: Three genuinely free image editors, three different trade-offs. Here's what each one actually gives you — and which one fits.
comparisons.verdict: For quick web graphics: Canva. For real photo editing without installing anything: Photopea. For the full Photoshop-class toolset you own forever: GIMP. All three are genuinely free — the choice is about workflow, not price.

comparisons.title: Best Free Video Editors Compared
comparisons.desc: DaVinci Resolve vs Blender vs OBS — the free video tools professionals actually use, compared honestly.
comparisons.intro: These aren't toy editors with watermarks — they're the tools used on real productions. Here's how they split the work.
comparisons.verdict: For video editing and color grading: DaVinci Resolve, no contest — it's the industry standard, free. For 3D animation and VFX: Blender. For live streaming and screen recording: OBS. They complement more than they compete.

comparisons.title: Best Free Streaming Services Compared
comparisons.desc: Tubi vs Pluto TV vs Kanopy vs Hoopla vs The Roku Channel — every genuinely free streaming option, ranked.
comparisons.intro: Five ways to watch movies and shows without a subscription or a credit card. Each one earns its free differently.
comparisons.verdict: For the biggest free catalog: Tubi. For channel-surfing like cable: Pluto TV. For art-house and documentaries ad-free: Kanopy (library card). For everything in one app — movies, audiobooks, comics: Hoopla (library card). Use all five; they're all free and they barely overlap.

comparisons.title: Free Tax Filing Compared
comparisons.desc: TurboTax Free vs FreeTaxUSA vs H&R Block Free vs Cash App Taxes — which one is actually free for YOUR return?
comparisons.intro: Four 'free' tax filing options with very different definitions of the word. Here's who qualifies, who gets squeezed, and who files every return free.
comparisons.verdict: FreeTaxUSA wins: free federal filing for every complexity level, flat $15 for state, no bait-and-switch. Cash App Taxes covers most returns completely free. TurboTax and H&R Block are free only for the simplest returns — and both are designed to upgrade you mid-flow.

comparisons.title: Free Password Managers Compared
comparisons.desc: Bitwarden vs LastPass free — one open-source champion vs one cautionary tale. The honest comparison.
comparisons.intro: Two free password managers with very different reputations. One syncs everywhere and was independently audited; the other restricts you to one device type and suffered a major breach.
comparisons.verdict: Bitwarden. It's not close. Free Bitwarden syncs across all devices, is open source, independently audited, and has never been breached. Free LastPass locks you to one device type and carries the weight of 2022. Switch today; the import takes minutes.

comparisons.title: Free VPNs Compared — The Honest Guide
comparisons.desc: Proton VPN (genuinely free) vs Hola (fake free) vs NordVPN (not free at all). The only VPN comparison that asks who's paying.
comparisons.intro: The question with free VPNs is never 'does it work' — it's 'who's paying for the servers.' Three answers, three very different verdicts.
comparisons.verdict: Proton VPN is the only honest answer: genuinely free, no data cap, funded by paid subscribers, independently audited. Hola historically monetized your bandwidth. NordVPN isn't free at all. For a free VPN, there is one choice.

comparisons.title: Free Office Suites Compared
comparisons.desc: LibreOffice vs Google Docs vs Microsoft 365 Online — three ways to write, calculate, and present for $0.
comparisons.intro: A desktop app you own, a cloud suite tied to Google, and Microsoft's own web apps — all free, all real, all different.
comparisons.verdict: For offline power with no account: LibreOffice. For collaboration and cloud-first workflow: Google. For Microsoft compatibility in a browser: Microsoft 365 Online. Most people should start with Google (already have the account) and reach for LibreOffice when they need offline or privacy.

comparisons.title: Free Messaging Apps Compared
comparisons.desc: Signal vs WhatsApp vs Telegram — all free, very different privacy models. Which one deserves your conversations?
comparisons.intro: Three billion-user messaging apps, all free, with encryption promises that mean very different things. The price is $0 everywhere; the privacy isn't.
comparisons.verdict: For privacy: Signal — end-to-end encrypted, nonprofit, no metadata collection. For reach: WhatsApp — three billion users, encrypted content but Meta collects metadata. For features and large groups: Telegram — but regular chats are NOT end-to-end encrypted by default. Know the trade-off you're making.

comparisons.title: Best Free Learning Platforms Compared
comparisons.desc: Khan Academy vs freeCodeCamp vs MIT OCW vs CS50 — the truly free education that rivals paid courses.
comparisons.intro: Four platforms where 'free' means actually free — no hidden tier, no audit-mode trick, no card. Here's what each one teaches best.
comparisons.verdict: For K–12 through college fundamentals: Khan Academy. For learning to code from zero to employable: freeCodeCamp. For university-depth self-study in any field: MIT OCW. For the single best intro to computer science: CS50. All are truly free. Use them together.

comparisons.title: Free Website Hosting Compared
comparisons.desc: Netlify vs GitHub vs Wix vs WordPress.com — which free hosting actually lets you build without a banner or a clock?
comparisons.intro: Four ways to put a website online for $0 — with very different definitions of 'yours.'
comparisons.verdict: For a clean site you fully own: Netlify (custom domain, no banner, drag-and-drop deploy). For developer projects and portfolios: GitHub Pages. For a drag-and-drop builder you don't mind wearing a banner: Wix. WordPress.com's free tier is the most restricted. Netlify + a $12 domain is the best free stack.

changelog.change: Free Score 82 → 74; the members claim corrected
changelog.detail: Our page said the free plan included unlimited members and called that unusually generous. Atlassian capped free Workspaces at 10 collaborators on 8 April 2024 — counting guests and pending invites — and a Workspace over the limit has its boards turned view-only with automations halted. The verdict stays Free forever, because the tier really is permanent and cardless, but the score drops: three hard fences, and an overage penalty that removes access you already had.

changelog.change: Split into .com and .org; free storage cut recorded
changelog.detail: Search data showed people asking 'is WordPress free' and landing on a page about WordPress.com only. The .org/.com distinction is the answer, so each now has its own verdict: the software Truly Free, the hosted service Free-ish. Also records that WordPress.com's free storage dropped from 3GB to 1GB.

Checked all 161 outbound listing links. Two FTC guidance pages had 404'd after a site restructure, and four products had moved domain: Anchor to Spotify for Creators, zoom.us to zoom.com, CS50 to its course page, and Google Digital Garage into Skillshop. The Digital Garage courses remain free.

changelog.change: Free tier confirmed closed to new customers
changelog.detail: Peacock stopped offering its free ad-supported tier to new customers in January 2023; existing accounts were grandfathered. Our listing still described the free tier as available, which was wrong for anyone signing up today. Re-verified and re-graded, free score 42 to 4.

changelog.change: DOJ settlement — $150M over cancellation dark patterns
changelog.detail: Adobe settled a Department of Justice lawsuit over hidden early-termination fees and obstructive cancellation flows: $75 million in free services to affected customers, $75 million to the DOJ. Customers charged the 50% exit fee between January 2019 and July 2025 may be eligible.
Ad-supported free streaming shut down December 31, 2025. Every plan now requires payment. Some older titles still surface on Tubi and Pluto TV.

changelog.change: Energy meter replaces hearts on mobile
changelog.detail: The new energy system drains even on correct answers, capping most free mobile users at a couple of lessons per day. Web version still runs the gentler hearts system.
Down from 2,000 contacts in 2021, then 500, now 250 with a 500-send monthly cap. Fourth cut since the Intuit acquisition.
One-on-one calls were previously unlimited on the free plan. Now all meetings hosted by free accounts cap at 40 minutes.
The Federal Trade Commission found Intuit's 'free' advertising deceptive — most filers who start the 'free' flow are forced into paid tiers mid-return.
Even paying Prime members now see ads unless they pay an additional ad-free upcharge — a second toll booth on a service already behind a paywall.
The ~25-generation free trial was suspended due to abuse and demand. As of July 2026 it has never returned to the main platform.

changelog.change: Free restricted to one device type
changelog.detail: Free users can now sync passwords on mobile OR desktop, not both — crippling the core purpose of a password manager. Drove mass migration to Bitwarden.
Attackers accessed encrypted password vaults. LastPass says strong master passwords protect users; security researchers noted weaker defaults on older accounts.
Intuit withdrew from the IRS Free File partnership that required genuine free filing for low-income taxpayers, making TurboTax's 'free' its own definition rather than the IRS's.
